label: CJEU C-252/21 — Meta Platforms v Bundeskartellamt — post-Brexit, not binding in the UK
body: 2. Where a user visits sites/apps revealing Art. 9 categories and that data is linked to the user's social-network account, processing by the operator must be regarded as "processing of special categories of personal data" under Art. 9(1) — prohibited unless an Art. 9(2) exception applies.

3. A user does not "manifestly make public" (Art. 9(2)(e)) data collected via cookies from third-party site visits. They do manifestly make public information they explicitly choose to make publicly accessible to an unlimited number of persons.

4. Art. 6(1)(b) (contract) covers processing only where it is objectively indispensable for a purpose integral to the contractual obligation — the main subject matter cannot be achieved without it. A tight necessity test.

5. Art. 6(1)(f) (legitimate interests) requires: (i) the LI was disclosed to users, (ii) processing is strictly necessary for that LI, and (iii) balancing favours the controller. Personalised advertising will rarely satisfy this in a dominant-platform context.
8. Dominance does not, as such, preclude valid consent, but is a key factor in assessing whether consent was freely given.

Why it matters: Tightened Art. 6(1)(b)/(f) for ad-tech. Confirmed the conditioned Art. 9 inference rule. Linked competition + data-protection enforcement. Respondent is the Bundeskartellamt (federal competition authority). Decided post-IP-completion-day: persuasive only, not binding, in UK courts.
